prize_parts.citation: for the theoretical prediction of the quantum spin Hall effect and Z2 topological insulators and its experimental observation in HgTe quantum wells

statement.case_for: Topological insulators introduced a classification of electronic matter by band-structure invariants rather than broken symmetry. The chain is unusually clear: Kane and Mele proposed the Z2 invariant and the quantum spin Hall state, and Molenkamp's group observed the helical edge transport in HgTe wells. Two decades of independent confirmation (transport, ARPES, many materials) make the discovery mature, and the concept has migrated into photonics, cold atoms and acoustics, which I take as a sign of conceptual depth, not of fashion. It also fits the statute better than a technology whose value lies mainly in engineering performance, because the discovery is a new principle. It complements the 2016 prize for topological phases, which concerned integer quantum Hall and Kosterlitz-Thouless physics, without repeating it.
statement.case_against: The credit is the strongest reservation. The experimental HgTe result followed the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang prediction, whose authors are not in the credited names (Zhang died in 2018), and the 3D topological-insulator work of Fu, Kane and Mele, Moore and Balents, and of Hasan's group, is also outside the list. A Kane-Mele-Molenkamp trio can be defended, but it will look incomplete to part of the community, and I cannot repair that within the supplied names. A second reservation is overlap with 2016, which some colleagues will say already covers topology in condensed matter.

responses.point: Kroll ranked the optical lattice clock (Katori, Ye) first as a clean, measurement-driven discovery with excellent timing, and ranked topological insulators only eighth because of contested allocation and remaining debate about clean edge transport.
responses.response: I agree that the lattice clock is a clean two-person prize with a clear idea and many independent confirmations, and I keep it as my first alternative. I disagree on two points. The redefinition of the second has not happened, and a prize for precision gains is mostly about engineering of a known principle after the Hall-Haensch and Wineland prizes. And the attribution problem in B039 is real but it concerns who else should be added, not whether Kane, Mele and Molenkamp made decisive and distinct contributions. Imperfect edge quantisation in HgTe is a known experimental limit, not a doubt about the topological classification.

responses.point: Johansson ranked B039 first as timely and arguably overdue, put the lattice clock second, and noted that the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang and 3D contributors lie outside the supplied credit.
responses.response: I agree with the ranking and with the maturity argument. I would go further on attribution than your opening did: the omission of BHZ is the main thing the committee has to be honest about in the citation. I would therefore word the citation around the quantum spin Hall effect and its observation, and not around topological insulators in general, so that it does not claim the 3D discoveries or the HgTe prediction for the three named people. I also note your field proximity to circuit QED and your decision to rank it only third, which seems right to me given the 2025 prize.

responses.point: Eriksson ranked B039 first and B035 (magic-angle graphene) second, calling the former a clear theory-to-experiment chain and the latter a striking case of theory guiding discovery, though possibly early.
responses.response: We agree on B039. On B035 I share the scientific admiration, but I am cautious: the origin of the superconductivity and the correlated states is still debated and the experiments are only eight years old, and the experimental credit (Cao, Fatemi, Dean and others) is spread beyond the supplied names. I would keep it as a second alternative for a later year and not pair it with B039 now. A two-part prize would also exceed the three-person limit with the credited names.

responses.point: Pearce, the chair, ranked IceCube neutrinos (Halzen) first as the opening of a new observational window, but called a single-name prize thin and arguably unfair given the collaboration and earlier pioneers.
responses.response: I share the reservation about a one-person prize for a collaboration-scale discovery, and I think it is a serious obstacle, not a detail, because the statute allows three laureates and the supplied credit uses only one. I do not rank B003 in my top choices for that reason and because I am less able to judge the source-identification evidence. If the committee wants an astrophysics prize, I would want to hear how the credit could be framed before supporting it.

uncertainties: Whether the committee can accept a Kane-Mele-Molenkamp configuration given the omission of Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang and the 3D topological-insulator discoverers.
Whether the 2016 topological-phases prize makes this recognition look like a repeat in the eyes of the committee.
Whether the committee prefers the lattice clock (B022) once the redefinition of the second is closer, and how much weight the discovery criterion gives to precision metrology.
I have not read the underlying nominations, so my assessment of credit rests on the supplied names and my own knowledge of the field.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile. My research (turbulence, stochastic processes, random matrices, neural networks) is not close to any shortlisted candidate, and none of the credited names appears among my documented co-authors or supervisors.
